the-betrothed: Walter Scott's contribution to his Tales of the Crusaders leaves the Holy Land for the Welsh border country. A Norman knight bound by a rash vow of betrothal must choose between honor and love amid the wars of the twelfth century. Though less famous than Ivanhoe, it shows Scott's romantic imagination working on his favorite themes of loyalty and chivalry.
ancient-china-simplified: Diplomat-scholar Edward Harper Parker distills thousands of years of Chinese history into a clear, readable survey. Dynasties, philosophers, and great events pass in review, explained for Western readers with no background in the subject. Though scholarship has moved on, the book remains an engaging first map of China's immense past.
the-earth-trembled: Edward Payson Roe sets this powerful novel against the Charleston earthquake of 1886, which shattered one of America's loveliest cities. Through the disaster he follows characters tested by terror, loss, and the chance to rebuild. Part disaster story, part moral tale, it shows Roe's gift for turning real events into moving fiction.
fanny-the-flower-girl-or-honesty-rewarde: Selina Bunbury's moral tales for children center on Fanny, the honest flower-girl whose virtue is rewarded. Additional stories reinforce lessons of kindness, truthfulness, and industry. Written in the earnest Victorian manner, the book shows how young readers were once taught right from wrong.
the-story-of-siegfried: James Baldwin retells the Norse legend of Siegfried — the dragon-slayer, the hero of the Nibelungen — for young readers. Gods, giants, and a cursed ring fill this stirring introduction to the North's greatest hero-tale. The myths that inspired Wagner, made thrillingly accessible.
